title: Finding left and right boundaries with half-integers
summary: In an integer array, locate the left and right boundaries of duplicate values using two absent half-integers.
context: The sorted integer array is nums = [1, 3, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 10, 12, 15], and the target element is target = 6 (occupying indices 2 through 6). Because every element in the array is an integer, the constructed half-integers target - 0.5 = 5.5 and target + 0.5 = 6.5 cannot appear in the array.
description: When closed-interval binary search looks for a target value absent from the array, the loop needs no equality branch; once the search interval becomes empty, pointer i necessarily points to the first element greater than that target, and pointer j necessarily points to the rightmost element smaller than that target. If no greater element exists, i = n; if no smaller element exists, j = -1, placing the corresponding pointer outside the array.

The left side of the figure shows that “Find the leftmost target” is “Equivalent” to “Search for target - 0.5” (5.5): when the search ends, j = 1 (pointing to 3) and i = 2 (pointing to the first element greater than 5.5, namely the leftmost 6), so returning i = 2 gives the left boundary. The right side shows that “Find the rightmost target” is “Equivalent” to “Search for target + 0.5” (6.5): when the search ends, j = 6 (pointing to the rightmost element smaller than 6.5, namely the rightmost 6) and i = 7 (pointing to 10), so returning j = 6 gives the right boundary.

frames.title: Finding left and right boundaries with half-integers
frames.explanation: This method relies on the premise that the input array contains only integers (if the array itself contained fractional numbers, ±0.5 could collide with an existing element and fail); in a general implementation where target might be absent from the array, you must still verify before returning that the index is in bounds and the element at that index equals target.
